claims.text: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy forms a poorly adherent, fast-growing, and spall-prone oxide scale at 1400°C in air.
Adding 0.3 wt% yttrium causes yttrium to segregate to the oxide–metal interface.
Yttrium segregation to the oxide–metal interface improves interfacial bonding.
Yttrium segregation to the oxide–metal interface reduces defects.
Yttrium acts as a reactive element that promotes protective-oxide nucleation.
The protective oxide formed after yttrium addition is likely alumina or a related compound.
Adding 0.3 wt% yttrium promotes formation of a continuous oxide layer.
The yttrium-promoted oxide adheres more strongly to the alloy substrate.
Stronger oxide-scale adhesion suppresses scale spallation.
The yttrium-promoted protective oxide slows oxygen permeation.
The yttrium-promoted oxide grows more slowly than the oxide on the untreated alloy.
Adding 0.3 wt% yttrium will reduce oxidation weight gain by at least 30% relative to the untreated alloy during 100 hours at 1400°C in air.
The yttrium-containing alloy will have a more continuous oxide scale than the untreated alloy after the specified exposure.
The proposed yttrium effect may not occur at lower temperatures.
The proposed yttrium effect may not occur under atmospheric compositions different from air.
The magnitude of oxidation improvement depends on the overall alloy composition.
The magnitude of oxidation improvement depends on processing conditions.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts both at least a 30% weight-gain reduction and improved scale adhesion, but the falsification rule uses an 'and' condition that requires both predictions to fail. A result in which only one predicted endpoint fails would contradict part of the hypothesis yet would not clearly falsify it under the stated rule.
